body.heading: The point of no return
paragraphs: Everything with mass has an escape velocity — the speed needed to leave it forever. For Earth it is about 11 kilometres per second. Squeeze a mass into a small enough space, and that speed rises past the speed of light itself.

That is a black hole. Its boundary, the event horizon, is the point of no return: cross it, and every path leads inward. Most black holes are born when a massive star collapses at the end of its life. Others, the supermassive ones, weigh millions or billions of Suns and sit at the centres of galaxies — including Sagittarius A*, the four-million-solar-mass black hole at the heart of our own Milky Way.

body.heading: Seeing the invisible
paragraphs: A black hole emits no light, so astronomers study it by its effects: stars whipping around an unseen mass, and gas heating to a brilliant glow as it spirals in.

In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope — a planet-wide network of radio dishes working as one — produced the first image of a black hole’s shadow, in the galaxy M87. In 2022 it did the same for our own Sagittarius A*. We cannot see the hole, but we can photograph its silhouette against the fire around it.

body.heading: Not cosmic vacuum cleaners
paragraphs: Despite the popular image, a black hole does not suck things in from afar. Far away, its gravity behaves like the gravity of anything else with the same mass — if the Sun were replaced by a black hole of equal mass, Earth’s orbit would not change at all.
The danger is only up close, past the point where light itself gives up. The rest is just gravity, doing what gravity does.

takeaway: A black hole is not a hole at all — it is mass packed so tightly that its gravity traps light itself, and we study it by the glow of everything around it.
